For two weeks Jatin hadn't shown up at the evening volleyball near the gurdwara in their Sangrur mohalla. When Amandeep asked, Jatin's mother only said, 'He sleeps all day. Eats like a sparrow.'
So on Thursday Amandeep stopped at the gate with two cups of tea from the dhaba. Jatin came out slowly, thinner, eyes puffy.
Amandeep didn't ask why. 'I'm fetching a tractor part from the market tomorrow at ten. Come for the ride? You don't have to talk.'
'Maybe,' Jatin said.
Jatin didn't come on Friday. Amandeep came back on Saturday with tea anyway, and again on Monday. On Monday, Jatin climbed onto the tractor.
Halfway to the market, Jatin said, 'I don't know what's wrong with me.'
Amandeep said, 'Then let's ask the doctor at the health centre together. I'll come.'

qa.q: What did Jatin's mother say about him?
qa.a: She said he sleeps all day and eats like a sparrow.

qa.q: What does Jatin's 'I don't know what's wrong with me' show?
qa.a: It shows he is confused and worn down by his low mood, and is finally trusting Amandeep enough to say so.

qa.q: What made Amandeep's approach work where a lecture might not have?
qa.a: Amandeep offered a plain task with no need to talk, kept coming back after the first no, and when Jatin opened up, offered to go to the doctor together.

qa.q: How might Jatin experience Amandeep returning with tea after the missed ride?
qa.a: Jatin probably felt that someone still wanted his company despite letting them down, which made saying yes less costly.

grounding: It shows a friend noticing someone has stopped coming out, returning steadily with a low-pressure invitation and suggesting a doctor for persistent low mood.

subtype: Stage 5: Deepening isolation and low mood [Observer]
passage:
In the university dorm in Osaka, Mina noticed that Kaito's door had stayed shut for most of two weeks. He used to cook curry for the whole floor on Fridays. Now the shared fridge held only his untouched carton of milk, and the kitchen no longer smelled of spices.
Mina didn't knock with a speech. On Friday she slipped a note under his door: "Making onigiri at 7. Too many for one person. No need to talk." He didn't come. On Saturday she knocked once and held up a warm box. He opened the door a crack, took it and said thank you.
On Sunday she knocked again. This time he sat in the kitchen for ten minutes, quiet. Before he left she said lightly, "The student health centre has a counsellor, if things stay heavy. I can walk there with you."
Kaito nodded slowly. "Maybe Tuesday."

qa.q: What did Kaito use to cook on Fridays?
qa.a: Curry for the whole floor.

qa.q: What was Mina feeling when she chose a note instead of a speech?
qa.a: Mina felt worried but careful, wanting to reach Kaito without putting pressure on him.

qa.q: Why does Mina's approach suit this stage?
qa.a: Low-pressure invitations repeated steadily, plus a gentle offer to walk to the counsellor, reach someone withdrawn without a lecture.

qa.q: What might Kaito feel when he sits in the kitchen for ten minutes?
qa.a: Kaito probably feels tired and low but a little comforted that someone kept coming back without demanding anything.

grounding: A dorm mate notices a friend has stopped coming out, offers simple low-pressure invitations, keeps returning and suggests a counsellor.

On the third floor of the engineering hostel, Tenzin noticed the pattern first. Karthik, who used to be the loudest voice at the carrom board, had stopped coming to the mess for dinner. His curtains stayed drawn at noon. Passing his room at 2 a.m., Tenzin could hear the same video playing on a loop.
The others said, "He'll snap out of it." Tenzin wasn't sure.
He didn't lecture. Each evening at eight he knocked: "Mess has rajma today. Coming?" Four nights Karthik said no. On the fifth he came, ate half a plate, said nothing, but stayed.
A week later, walking back, Karthik admitted he had felt flat for a month and couldn't make himself care about anything. Tenzin said, "That sounds heavy. The health centre has a counsellor and a doctor. Want me to come with you tomorrow?"
Karthik looked at his shoes. "Okay. Tomorrow."

qa.q: What did the mess have when Tenzin knocked?
qa.a: Rajma.

qa.q: What did Tenzin feel when the others said Karthik would snap out of it?
qa.a: Tenzin felt uneasy and worried, unconvinced that the withdrawal would pass on its own.

qa.q: What did Tenzin do well?
qa.a: He knocked every evening with a simple invitation, never lectured, and offered to go with Karthik to the counsellor and doctor.

qa.q: What might Karthik have felt coming to the mess on the fifth night?
qa.a: He probably felt drained and shy, but a little less alone because Tenzin kept coming back.

grounding: A hostel mate notices a friend withdrawing, keeps offering simple invitations and, when the low mood persists, offers to go to a counsellor together.

passage:
Dear Uday,
You haven't come to Sunday cycling in six weeks, and your phone goes straight to messages. Your roommate says you mostly stay in your room. I'm not writing to scold you. I just miss you, and I'm a bit worried.
I know you. When things get heavy, you go quiet and tell yourself you're sparing everyone. You don't have to spare me. You never have.
So here's a very small invitation, no pressure: I'll be at the chai stall outside Gate 2 at five on Thursday, like old times. If you come, great. If you don't, I'll be there again next Thursday.
And one more thing, gently: if this low feeling has been sitting on you for weeks, it might help to see the campus counsellor or a doctor. I can come with you, or just wait outside.
Your friend,
Shreya

qa.q: Where will Shreya be on Thursday?
qa.a: At the chai stall outside Gate 2 at five.

qa.q: What is Shreya feeling while writing?
qa.a: Shreya feels worried and misses Uday, but is careful not to scold or pressure.

qa.q: Why is Shreya's invitation a wise one?
qa.a: It is small, low-pressure and repeated every Thursday, with a gentle offer to go to the counsellor or doctor together.

qa.q: What might Uday feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Uday may feel seen and relieved that a friend still cares, which could make reaching back a little easier.

grounding: A friend notices someone has stopped coming out and writes a low-pressure, repeated invitation, gently suggesting a counsellor or doctor.

First he stopped coming to the mess for dinner. Then he skipped our Friday movie on the terrace, which he started. His room light is on at four. When I asked, he said, 'I'm fine, just busy.' My first idea was to give him a speech about taking care of himself. I didn't. I just knocked on Monday and said, 'Going for chai, want to come? No worries if not.' He said no. I knocked again Wednesday. No. Thursday he came, sat for ten minutes, barely spoke. Friday he came again. It's been three weeks like this, though, and he still looks flat. I think I have to tell him, gently, that talking to the campus doctor or counsellor isn't a big deal."

qa.a: Manoj may feel both awkward and quietly grateful, because saying yes is hard but the steady invitations show someone still wants him there.
